subject: Physics
title: Faraday's Discovery: Making Power from Magnetism
hook: A changing magnetic field can generate electricity without a battery. Anjali swings a magnet near a coil and watches a meter jump.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student discovering electromagnetic induction with a coil and magnet

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor explaining Faraday's law and Lenz's law

slides.title: Electromagnetic Induction
slides.storyContext: Anjali swings a bar magnet toward a coil connected to an ammeter. Mysteriously, the meter needle deflects—without any battery!

slides.title: The Swinging Magnet
slides.storyContext: In her physics lab in Mumbai, Anjali holds a bar magnet near a coil wired to an ammeter. When she swings the magnet toward the coil, the meter jumps—current flows! When she holds the magnet still, the current stops. 'Ravi uncle, how can a magnet make electricity?' she asks. Ravi smiles: 'Faraday discovered that a *changing* magnetic field induces an electric field. This is the secret behind generators, transformers, and all AC power.'

slides.title: Magnetic Flux

points.label: Flux definition
points.text: Magnetic flux Φ (or Φ_B) is the magnetic field passing through a surface: Φ = ∫ B · dA. For uniform field perpendicular to area A: Φ = B A. Unit: weber (Wb) = tesla·m^2 (T·m^2).

points.label: Flux through a coil
points.text: For a coil with N turns, area A, in uniform field B at angle θ to normal: Φ = N B A cos(θ). Maximum when B is perpendicular to coil (θ = 0); zero when B is parallel to coil plane (θ = 90°).

points.label: Changing flux
points.text: Time-varying flux Φ(t) is key to induction. The rate of change dΦ/dt drives induced EMF.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic flux is how much field is threading through a surface. More field or bigger area means more flux. Angling the field reduces flux (cos effect).

slides.title: Worked Example: Flux Through a Rotating Coil

example.problem: A square coil with side 0.1 m (area A = 0.01 m²) rotates in a uniform magnetic field B = 2 T. The axis of rotation is perpendicular to B. At time t, the angle between B and the normal to the coil is θ(t) = ωt, where ω = 10 rad/s. Find the flux as a function of time and sketch it.
example.solution: Φ(t) = B A cos(θ(t)) = 2 × 0.01 × cos(10t) = 0.02 cos(10t) Wb. At t=0, Φ = 0.02 Wb (maximum). At t=π/20 s, θ = π/2, so Φ = 0 (field parallel to coil plane). At t=π/10 s, θ = π, so Φ = −0.02 Wb (reversed). The flux oscillates sinusoidally from +0.02 to −0.02 Wb with period T = 2π/ω ≈ 0.628 s.

slides.inSimpleWords: As a coil rotates, the flux through it oscillates. Maximum flux occurs when the field is perpendicular to the coil face; zero when parallel to the plane.

slides.title: Why Changing Flux Matters
slides.storyContext: Anjali tries an experiment: holding the magnet perfectly still near the coil. The ammeter shows zero. 'No current!' she exclaims. Ravi nods. 'Exactly, Anjali. A *static* magnetic field, no matter how strong, induces no current. But the moment you move the magnet—changing the flux—current flows. This is the heart of Faraday's law. Generators work by rotating a coil, changing the flux continuously, which drives a current. Static field = no induction. Changing field = induction. Simple rule.'

slides.title: Faraday's Law of Induction

points.label: The law
points.text: Induced EMF in a circuit equals the negative rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = −dΦ/dt. For N-turn coil: ε = −N dΦ/dt. Unit: volt (V).

points.label: Negative sign (Lenz's law insight)
points.text: The negative sign means induced EMF opposes the change in flux. If flux increases, induced EMF creates current to oppose it (pushes field out). If flux decreases, induced current tries to preserve it (pulls field in).

points.label: Physical interpretation
points.text: The induced EMF arises from a changing electric field generated by the changing magnetic field. This electric field accelerates charges in the circuit, creating current.

example.problem: A coil has N = 100 turns, area A = 0.02 m², and is in a uniform field B = 0.5 T perpendicular to the coil. The field decreases uniformly from 0.5 T to 0 T in Δt = 0.1 s. Find the induced EMF and direction (by Lenz's law).
example.solution: Initial flux Φ_i = N B A = 100 × 0.5 × 0.02 = 1 Wb. Final flux Φ_f = 0. Change ΔΦ = Φ_f − Φ_i = −1 Wb. Rate dΦ/dt = ΔΦ/Δt = −1/0.1 = −10 Wb/s. Induced EMF ε = −dΦ/dt = −(−10) = +10 V. Positive EMF means the induced current flows in a direction to create a magnetic field in the same direction as the decreasing external field (Lenz opposes the decrease).

slides.inSimpleWords: Faraday's law: changing magnetic flux generates electric voltage. Faster change means higher voltage. Lenz's law says the induced current always opposes the change.

slides.title: Lenz's Law in Action: The Magnetic Brake
slides.storyContext: Ravi pushes a magnet into a copper tube, and Anjali feels resistance—the magnet slows down dramatically! 'That's Lenz's law at work,' Ravi explains. 'The changing flux induces currents in the tube (eddy currents) that create a magnetic field opposing the magnet's motion. The magnet must do work against this opposition. Energy is neither lost nor gained; the kinetic energy of the magnet converts to heat in the tube's resistance. This is how magnetic brakes work in trains and elevators!'

slides.title: Worked Example: EMF in a Moving Conductor

example.problem: A conducting rod of length L = 0.5 m slides along parallel rails separated by 0.5 m in a perpendicular magnetic field B = 1 T. The rod moves with constant velocity v = 2 m/s. Calculate the motional EMF, current (circuit resistance R = 10 Ω), and the magnetic force on the rod.
example.solution: Motional EMF: ε = B L v = 1 × 0.5 × 2 = 1 V. Current: I = ε/R = 1/10 = 0.1 A. Force on rod: F = B I L = 1 × 0.1 × 0.5 = 0.05 N (opposing motion). Power: P_mech = F × v = 0.05 × 2 = 0.1 W (work input). P_elec = I² R = (0.1)² × 10 = 0.1 W (dissipated). Energy is conserved: mechanical work input = electrical energy dissipated.

slides.inSimpleWords: Moving a conductor perpendicular to a magnetic field induces voltage (EMF = BLv). The resulting current experiences a force opposing the motion, so you must do work to keep it moving.

slides.title: Motional EMF and AC Generators

points.label: Simple motional EMF
points.text: A rod of length L moving perpendicular to B with velocity v generates EMF = B L v.

points.label: Rotating coil (AC generator)
points.text: A rectangular coil (N turns, area A) rotates in uniform B field. Flux Φ(t) = NBA cos(ωt) where ω = 2πf. Induced EMF ε(t) = NBA ω sin(ωt) = ε₀ sin(ωt) with peak ε₀ = NBA ω.

points.label: Generator equations
points.text: ε₀ = NBA × 2πf. For India (f = 50 Hz): ε₀ = NBA × 314. RMS voltage ε_rms = ε₀ / √2. Home voltage 230 V RMS → peak ≈ 325 V.

slides.inSimpleWords: Spinning a coil in a magnetic field generates alternating voltage. Faster spin or stronger field means higher peak voltage. This is how power plants make electricity.

slides.title: Worked Example: AC Generator Output

example.problem: A generator has N = 500 turns, A = 0.1 m², B = 0.8 T, rotating at f = 50 Hz. Calculate peak EMF, RMS EMF, and the current delivered to a 100 Ω load.
example.solution: Peak EMF: ε₀ = NBA × 2πf = 500 × 0.8 × 0.1 × 2π × 50 ≈ 500 × 0.8 × 0.1 × 314 = 12,560 V ≈ 12.6 kV. RMS EMF: ε_rms = ε₀/√2 ≈ 8.9 kV. Current (at RMS): I_rms = ε_rms / R = 8900 / 100 = 89 A. This voltage would power many homes after stepping down through transformers.

slides.inSimpleWords: AC generators produce voltage proportional to the number of turns, magnetic field strength, coil area, and rotation speed. Faster rotation or more turns means higher voltage.

slides.title: Self-Inductance and Back-EMF

points.label: Self-inductance L
points.text: When current I in a coil changes, it creates changing flux through itself, inducing a back-EMF: ε_back = −L (dI/dt). L = N Φ / I (henries, H). Opposes the change (Lenz's law).

points.label: Practical consequence
points.text: Inductors resist sudden changes in current. Switching off an inductive circuit abruptly can generate dangerous voltage spikes.

points.label: Energy storage
points.text: Inductor stores magnetic energy: U = (1/2) L I². This energy must be dissipated or converted when the circuit is broken.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inductors store energy in their magnetic field and resist changes in current. Suddenly breaking an inductive circuit releases stored energy as a high voltage spike.

slides.title: Worked Example: Inductor Voltage Spike

example.problem: An inductor with L = 0.2 H carries steady current I = 5 A. If the current is suddenly cut off in Δt = 0.01 s, calculate the induced back-EMF and the energy released.
example.solution: Back-EMF magnitude: |ε_back| = L |dI/dt| = 0.2 × (5/0.01) = 0.2 × 500 = 100 V. Energy stored: U = (1/2) L I² = 0.5 × 0.2 × (5)² = 2.5 J. This high voltage (100 V) appears across the switching device when the circuit breaks, potentially causing arcing or damping. The 2.5 J must dissipate as heat, spark, or electromagnetic radiation—dangerous if not managed!

slides.inSimpleWords: Cutting current through an inductor creates a high voltage spike. Industrial switches use protection circuits (diodes, resistors) to safely dissipate this energy.

slides.title: Mutual Inductance and Transformers

points.label: Mutual inductance M
points.text: Primary coil (N_p turns) carries current I_p, creating flux Φ through secondary coil (N_s turns). Secondary EMF: ε_s = −M (dI_p/dt). M = N_s Φ / I_p (henries).

points.label: Transformer principle
points.text: Ideal transformer couples primary and secondary through shared flux. Voltage ratio: V_s / V_p = N_s / N_p. Current ratio: I_s / I_p = N_p / N_s (inverse).

points.label: Power conservation
points.text: Ideal transformer conserves power: V_p I_p = V_s I_s. No power loss in coupling or core (unrealistic but useful approximation).

slides.inSimpleWords: Transformers scale voltage and current for efficient transmission and safe distribution. Step-up transformers increase voltage (decrease current) for long-distance transmission; step-down transformers reduce voltage for homes.

slides.title: Worked Example: Transformer Design

example.problem: A transformer steps down 230 V AC to 12 V AC. Primary has N_p = 1000 turns. (a) Find secondary turns N_s. (b) If primary draws I_p = 1 A, find secondary current and power. (c) Compare to non-ideal transformer with 5% loss.
example.solution: (a) N_s = N_p × (V_s/V_p) = 1000 × (12/230) ≈ 52 turns. (b) Ideal: I_s = V_p I_p / V_s = 230 × 1 / 12 ≈ 19.2 A. Power: P = V_s I_s = 12 × 19.2 = 230 W. (c) Non-ideal with 5% loss: P_out = 230 × (1 − 0.05) = 218.5 W. I_s = 218.5 / 12 ≈ 18.2 A. Real transformers lose power to core heating and wire resistance.

slides.inSimpleWords: Transformers scale voltage inversely with current. A step-down 230V→12V transformer increases current by the inverse ratio (~19×). Real transformers have 90-99% efficiency.

slides.title: Worked Example: Induced EMF in a Sliding Loop

example.problem: A rectangular loop (length L = 0.3 m, width w = 0.2 m) moves at velocity v = 2 m/s into a perpendicular magnetic field B = 1.5 T. Calculate the induced EMF as the loop enters the field (leading edge cutting field lines) and when fully inside (no change).
example.solution: Leading edge entering: EMF = B L v = 1.5 × 0.3 × 2 = 0.9 V (voltage induced as the front of loop cuts field). Fully inside: dΦ/dt = 0 (flux constant once fully in), so EMF = 0 V. This explains why motors generate back-EMF only during acceleration or deceleration, not at constant speed.

slides.inSimpleWords: EMF is induced whenever flux changes. As a conductor cuts field lines (entering or leaving), EMF is generated. Once fully in a uniform field moving steadily, no more EMF.

slides.title: Wireless Power Transfer
slides.storyContext: Anjali's new phone has wireless charging—no cable! Ravi explains: 'A coil in the charger creates a time-varying magnetic field. Your phone's receiver coil detects the changing flux and, by Faraday's law, generates current to charge the battery. Same principle as a transformer, but with air gap instead of iron core. Induction across space.'

slides.title: Wireless Power Transfer via Mutual Inductance

points.label: Mutual inductance M
points.text: Primary coil (transmitter) oscillates at frequency f. Secondary coil (receiver) in its magnetic field experiences changing flux, inducing EMF ε = −M dI/dt.

points.label: Coupling coefficient
points.text: k = M / √(L₁L₂). For air gap: k ~ 0.1–0.3 (loose coupling). For iron core: k ~ 0.95 (tight coupling, like transformer).

points.label: Efficiency
points.text: Power transfer efficiency η = (kQ₁Q₂) / ((1 + k²)²), where Q is quality factor. Short range, high frequency (MHz) maximize efficiency.

slides.inSimpleWords: Wireless chargers use mutual inductance: changing current in transmitter coil induces voltage in receiver coil, transferring power across air gap.

slides.title: Worked Example: Induction Cooktop

example.problem: An induction cooktop coil (L₁ = 10 μH, oscillating at f = 20 kHz) sits beneath a metal pot (modeled as L₂ = 5 μH, R = 0.1 Ω). Mutual inductance M ≈ 1 μH. If primary current is I₁ = 50 A, find induced EMF in pot and power dissipated.
example.solution: Induced EMF: ε₂ = M dI₁/dt. dI₁/dt = I₀ ω cos(ωt) ≈ 50 × 2π × 20,000 ≈ 6.28 × 10^6 A/s (at zero crossing). ε₂ = 10^-6 × 6.28 × 10^6 ≈ 6.3 V. Pot impedance Z = R + jωL₂ ≈ 0.1 + j(2π × 20,000 × 5 × 10^-6) ≈ 0.1 + j0.63 Ω. Current in pot I₂ ≈ 6.3 / 0.63 ≈ 10 A. Power dissipated: P = I₂² R ≈ (10)² × 0.1 ≈ 10 W (modest—real cooktops use tighter coupling and higher power).

slides.inSimpleWords: Induction cooktops use mutual inductance to induce current in the pot, heating it via resistance. No flame, no direct contact—pure electromagnetic induction.

slides.title: Transformers in Power Distribution
slides.storyContext: Ravi takes Anjali on a school field trip to a power substation. They see massive transformers, oil-cooled and humming. 'Each step transforms voltage and current for the next stage of distribution,' he explains. 'Generator output (13 kV, high current) → step-up to 400 kV (low current, minimal loss) → substation steps down to 11 kV → local transformer drops to 440 V for buildings → final step-down to 230 V for homes. Each stage optimized by Faraday's law and the transformer ratio.'

slides.title: Losses in Real Transformers

points.label: Copper loss (I² R)
points.text: Primary and secondary windings have resistance. Power loss: P_Cu = I_primary² R_p + I_secondary² R_s. Minimized by using thick, low-resistance wire.

points.label: Core loss (hysteresis + eddy currents)
points.text: Magnetic core loses energy due to molecular friction (hysteresis) and induced eddy currents. Reduced by using laminated core (thin sheets to break eddy current loops) and soft iron.

points.label: Efficiency
points.text: Real transformer efficiency η ≈ 95–99% (depending on size and design). Small transformers ~95%, large power transformers ~99%.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real transformers have two types of loss: copper (wire resistance) and core (magnetic friction + eddy currents). Design minimizes both for maximum efficiency.

points.text: A copper disc (radius R = 0.2 m) rotates at ω = 50 rad/s in a perpendicular magnetic field B = 1 T. A contact at the center and rim completes a circuit through a load R_L = 50 Ω. Calculate the motional EMF between center and rim, current, power dissipated in load, and torque required to keep the disc spinning.

example.problem: Find EMF, current, power, and torque.
example.solution: EMF between center and rim: ε = (1/2) B ω R² = 0.5 × 1 × 50 × (0.2)² = 0.5 × 50 × 0.04 = 1 V. Current: I = ε / R_L = 1 / 50 = 0.02 A. Power in load: P = I² R_L = (0.02)² × 50 = 0.02 W. Torque required: τ = B I × (2R/3) (average lever arm) ≈ 1 × 0.02 × (2 × 0.2 / 3) ≈ 0.00267 N·m. This is a homopolar generator—no brushes or slip rings needed, but low voltage output.

points.text: A power plant generates 10 kW at 100 V. It must be transmitted 1 km through copper wire (resistance 0.1 Ω per 100 m, so total R = 1 Ω). Compare power loss in two scenarios: (a) direct transmission at 100 V; (b) step-up to 10 kV, transmit, then step-down to 100 V. Assume ideal transformers.

example.problem: Calculate power loss and efficiency in each case.
example.solution: (a) Direct at 100 V: I = P/V = 10,000/100 = 100 A. P_loss = I² R = 100² × 1 = 10,000 W = 10 kW. Efficiency = 0% (all power lost!). (b) Step-up to 10 kV: I_primary = 100 A. I_secondary = (V_p/V_s) × I_p = (100/10,000) × 100 = 1 A (due to step-up). P_loss = 1² × 1 = 1 W. After step-down: P_delivered = 10 kW at 100 V. Efficiency ≈ 99.99%. Higher voltage transmission dramatically reduces losses (I² R scaling).

slides.title: What You've Learned: Electromagnetic Induction

points.text: Magnetic flux Φ = B A cos(θ); measured in webers (Wb). Flux through N-turn coil: Φ = N B A cos(θ).
Faraday's law: induced EMF ε = −dΦ/dt. Lenz's law: induced current opposes the flux change causing it.
Motional EMF: ε = B L v (moving rod). Rotating coil: ε = NBA ω sin(ωt) (AC generator).
Self-inductance L and back-EMF ε = −L (dI/dt) govern inductor behavior. Stores energy U = (1/2) L I².
Transformers: mutual inductance couples primary and secondary. V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p; I_s/I_p = N_p/N_s.
Step-up transformers reduce transmission loss. Power lines use 400 kV (vs 13 kV generation) to minimize I² R loss.
Induction powers generators, motors, transformers, and wireless power transfer. Faraday's law is fundamental to all electrical engineering.

slides.inSimpleWords: Electromagnetic induction converts motion and changing magnetic flux into electricity. Transformers leverage it to move power across the grid efficiently. This is the foundation of modern power systems.

slides.title: The Eddy Current Brake Experiment
slides.storyContext: Ravi demonstrates eddy currents by dropping a magnet down a copper tube. It falls slowly, resisting gravity! 'The changing flux through the tube induces currents (eddy currents), which create a magnetic field opposing the magnet's motion,' Ravi explains. 'This is why elevators and trains can brake magnetically—no friction, silent, efficient. Lenz's law in action: the system always opposes the change.'

slides.title: Eddy Currents and Damping

points.label: What are eddy currents?
points.text: Circular currents induced in conductors by changing magnetic flux. Follow Lenz's law: flow direction creates field opposing the flux change.

points.label: Magnetic damping
points.text: Eddy currents dissipate energy as heat in conductor resistance. Result: objects moving through B field experience drag force F ∝ B² v (velocity-dependent braking).

points.label: Applications
points.text: Magnetic brakes in trains and elevators. Eddy current separators in recycling. Damping in instruments and meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Eddy currents are induced loops that oppose flux changes and dissipate energy. They create drag—the basis of magnetic braking.

slides.title: The Legacy of Faraday's Discovery
slides.storyContext: Anjali now understands why her school's solar panels have an inverter, why power lines buzz at 50 Hz, and why her physics teacher always says 'The magnet doesn't care if you move toward it or away—only the change matters.' She writes in her journal: 'Faraday figured this out 200 years ago without transistors, computers, or oscilloscopes. All he had was a coil, a magnet, and curiosity. Today, 8 billion people have electricity because of his insight. Changing flux—that's the entire world. Every hydroelectric dam, every wind turbine, every generator relies on this one principle: change magnetic flux, get electricity.'

subject: Physics
title: AC Power in Your Home
hook: Your ceiling fan runs on AC current that reverses 50 times per second. Anjali discovers how RMS voltage, impedance, and resonance govern the devices in her home.

characters.name: Anjali
characters.role: Student measuring voltage and current in AC circuits

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Tutor explaining phasors, impedance, and power factor

slides.title: Alternating Current
slides.storyContext: Anjali's home runs on 50 Hz AC current. But what does that mean? Ravi shows her with an oscilloscope: 'The voltage sine wave reverses 50 times per second.'

slides.title: AC in Every Outlet
slides.storyContext: Anjali plugs her phone charger into an outlet in Delhi and wonders: why AC, not DC like a battery? Ravi explains: 'AC (alternating current) at 230 V, 50 Hz comes from India's power grid. Generators make AC by rotating coils in magnetic fields—it's natural. AC is easy to step up and down with transformers, so we can transmit power across the country without huge losses. Your charger converts it to DC inside.'

image.alt: AC in Every Outlet — Alternating Current

slides.title: AC Voltage and Current Fundamentals

points.label: Sinusoidal form
points.text: AC voltage V(t) = V₀ sin(ωt + φ), where V₀ is peak voltage (amplitude), ω = 2πf is angular frequency (rad/s), f is frequency (Hz), φ is phase (rad). In India: f = 50 Hz, ω ≈ 314 rad/s, nominal voltage 230 V.

points.label: RMS value (root-mean-square)
points.text: For sinusoidal signal: V_rms = V₀ / √2 ≈ 0.707 V₀. Similarly I_rms = I₀ / √2. Meters display RMS values. Home voltage 230 V (RMS) corresponds to peak V₀ ≈ 325 V.

points.label: Period and frequency
points.text: Period T = 1/f. For f = 50 Hz: T = 0.02 s = 20 ms. One complete cycle every 20 milliseconds.

example.problem: Home voltage in India is 230 V (RMS). Calculate peak voltage, period, and peak power dissipated in a 100 W resistive load.
example.solution: V₀ = V_rms × √2 = 230 × √2 ≈ 325 V. Period T = 1/f = 1/50 = 0.02 s = 20 ms. For resistive load: P_avg = V_rms I_rms = V_rms² / R = (230)² / 230 ≈ 230 W (wait, recalculate: if P = 100 W, then R = V_rms²/P = 230²/100 = 529 Ω). Peak power: P_peak = V₀² / R = (325)² / 529 ≈ 200 W (twice average, since P ∝ V²).

slides.inSimpleWords: AC voltage oscillates sinusoidally. Meters show RMS (effective value), which does the same heating work as an equivalent DC voltage. Peak voltage is √2 times higher.

slides.title: Why RMS? The Energy Perspective
slides.storyContext: Ravi connects a heating element to an AC outlet. Anjali watches it glow red-hot. 'If this were supplied peak voltage (325 V), it would burn out instantly,' Ravi says. 'But we supply RMS (230 V), which delivers the same heating power as 230 V DC over time. RMS is the "effective" voltage—it accounts for the oscillation and gives us the heat (or power) we actually use. That's why meters, power companies, and power ratings all use RMS.'

slides.title: Average Power in AC Circuits

points.label: Instantaneous vs. average power
points.text: Instantaneous power: p(t) = v(t) × i(t) (oscillates rapidly). Average power: P = V_rms I_rms cos(φ), where φ is phase difference between voltage and current.

points.label: Power factor
points.text: cos(φ) is the power factor (PF). For purely resistive load: PF = 1 (voltage and current in phase). For inductive or capacitive: PF < 1 (power is "wasted" in reactive component).

points.label: Energy per cycle
points.text: Energy per cycle = P × T = P / f. For P = 230 W at f = 50 Hz: E = 230 / 50 = 4.6 J per cycle.

slides.inSimpleWords: Average power in AC is V_rms × I_rms × cos(phase). If voltage and current are out of phase (inductive/capacitive load), less of the current actually does work.

slides.title: Worked Example: Peak vs RMS Voltage and Power

example.problem: An AC outlet supplies 230 V (RMS) at 50 Hz. A purely resistive device draws 500 W. Calculate (a) peak voltage, (b) RMS current, (c) peak current, (d) resistance, (e) peak power dissipation.
example.solution: (a) V₀ = 230√2 ≈ 325 V. (b) I_rms = P / V_rms = 500 / 230 ≈ 2.17 A. (c) I₀ = I_rms × √2 ≈ 3.07 A. (d) R = V_rms / I_rms = 230 / 2.17 ≈ 106 Ω. (e) P_peak = V₀ I₀ = 325 × 3.07 ≈ 998 W ≈ 1000 W (twice average, confirming P_avg = 500 W). Note: instantaneous power oscillates between 0 and 1000 W at 100 Hz (twice the line frequency).

slides.inSimpleWords: Instantaneous AC power oscillates at twice the line frequency. Average power is half the peak, which is why we use RMS values (they give average power directly).

slides.title: AC in Resistive, Inductive, and Capacitive Circuits

points.label: Resistor (R)
points.text: Voltage and current in phase (phase difference φ = 0°). Impedance Z_R = R (ohms). Power: P = V_rms I_rms = I_rms² R (all real power).

points.label: Inductor (L)
points.text: Voltage leads current by 90° (φ = +90°). Inductive reactance X_L = ωL = 2πfL (ohms). Impedance Z_L = jωL (imaginary). Current lags voltage.

points.label: Capacitor (C)
points.text: Current leads voltage by 90° (φ = −90°). Capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(ωC) (ohms). Impedance Z_C = −j/(ωC). Current leads voltage.

slides.inSimpleWords: Resistors consume power (heating). Inductors delay current (inertia). Capacitors lead current (charge/discharge). Each component has different phase behavior.

slides.title: Worked Example: Inductor and Capacitor Reactance

example.problem: At f = 50 Hz: (a) An inductor L = 0.1 H. Find X_L. (b) A capacitor C = 100 μF. Find X_C. (c) If 230 V is applied across each alone, find current in each and the phase relationship.
example.solution: (a) X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.1 ≈ 31.4 Ω. (b) X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 50 × 100 × 10^-6) ≈ 31.8 Ω. (c) For inductor: I_L = V / X_L = 230 / 31.4 ≈ 7.3 A (lagging voltage by 90°). For capacitor: I_C = V × ωC = 230 × 2π × 50 × 100 × 10^-6 ≈ 7.2 A (leading voltage by 90°). Interesting: both allow same current (~7.2 A), but in opposite phase! They could cancel each other if in series at resonance.

slides.inSimpleWords: Inductors and capacitors both impede AC, but inductors lag while capacitors lead. They have opposite phase shifts and can cancel each other.

slides.title: Series RLC Circuit and Impedance

points.label: Total impedance
points.text: For R, L, C in series: Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²] (ohms). Phase angle: tan(φ) = (X_L − X_C) / R.

points.label: Resonance condition
points.text: At resonance frequency f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)), inductive and capacitive reactances cancel: X_L = X_C. Impedance Z_min = R, current I_max = V/R, and phase φ = 0 (PF = 1).

points.label: Quality factor Q
points.text: Q = ω₀L / R = 1 / (ω₀RC) = X_L / R at resonance. Higher Q means sharper resonance, narrower bandwidth.

example.problem: RLC circuit: R = 100 Ω, L = 0.5 H, C = 100 μF, driven at f = 50 Hz. Find Z, φ, and I. Then find resonance frequency and Q.

slides.inSimpleWords: RLC circuits have a resonance frequency where L and C cancel out, leaving only R. At resonance, impedance is minimum and current is maximum.

slides.title: Resonance in Music and Circuits
slides.storyContext: Anjali plays a sitar, and Ravi asks: 'When you pluck a string, which frequency rings the loudest?' 'The natural frequency,' she answers. 'Exactly!' Ravi smiles. 'The same principle applies to AC circuits. At resonance, the circuit responds with maximum current and power transfer. Radio and TV tuners use resonant circuits—you adjust L and C until resonance matches the broadcast frequency. That's why turning a dial on an old radio tunes in different stations!'

slides.title: Power Factor and Reactive vs Real Power

points.label: Real power (P)
points.text: Power actually consumed (converted to heat, work): P = V_rms I_rms cos(φ) = I_rms² R (watts, W). Only resistive component dissipates energy.

points.label: Reactive power (Q)
points.text: Power oscillating between source and inductors/capacitors: Q = V_rms I_rms sin(φ) = I_rms² X (volt-amperes reactive, VAR). No net energy transfer, just sloshes back and forth.

points.label: Apparent power and power factor
points.text: Apparent power: S = V_rms I_rms (volt-amperes, VA). Power factor: PF = cos(φ) = P/S. Ideal PF = 1; lagging PF for inductors; leading PF for capacitors.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real power (P) is what you pay for. Reactive power (Q) wastes current without doing work. Power factor measures efficiency: PF = 1 is ideal, PF < 1 means wasted current.

slides.title: Worked Example: Motor Power Factor

example.problem: A 1 kW motor draws 5 A at 230 V, 50 Hz. Calculate real power, reactive power, apparent power, and power factor.
example.solution: Apparent power: S = V_rms × I_rms = 230 × 5 = 1150 VA. Real power: P = 1000 W (given rating). Power factor: PF = P/S = 1000/1150 ≈ 0.87. Phase angle: φ = arccos(0.87) ≈ 29.5°. Reactive power: Q = S × sin(φ) = 1150 × sin(29.5°) ≈ 566 VAR. Only 87% of the current does useful work; 13% is wasted in magnetic field oscillation (inductance of motor windings).

slides.inSimpleWords: Inductive motors have low power factor (typically 0.7–0.9). You pay for apparent power (1150 VA) but use only real power (1000 W). The difference wastes current.

slides.title: Phasor Representation
slides.storyContext: Ravi draws a diagram with vectors rotating. 'Voltage and current in AC circuits have phase differences. A phasor is a rotating vector representing amplitude and phase. Voltage phasor points along 0°; current phasor lags or leads. This visual tool makes AC circuit math much simpler—we use complex numbers instead of time-domain equations.'

slides.title: Worked Example: Phasor Analysis of RLC Circuit

example.problem: RLC: R = 50 Ω, X_L = 100 Ω, X_C = 30 Ω. Applied voltage V = 100 ∠0° V (reference). Find impedance phasor, current phasor, and phase angle.
example.solution: Impedance phasor: Z = R + j(X_L − X_C) = 50 + j(100 − 30) = 50 + j70 Ω. |Z| = √(50² + 70²) ≈ 86.0 Ω. Phase: φ = arctan(70/50) ≈ 54.5°. Current phasor: I = V/Z = 100∠0° / 86.0∠54.5° ≈ 1.16∠−54.5° A. Voltage leads current by 54.5° (inductive). Real power: P = |I|² R = (1.16)² × 50 ≈ 67 W.

slides.inSimpleWords: Phasors represent AC quantities as vectors in complex plane. Impedance adds resistance and reactance as perpendicular components. Math is cleaner than time-domain.

points.text: A factory has an inductive load drawing 100 kW at power factor 0.8 (lagging). Electricity tariff costs Rs. 8 per kVA-month of apparent power and penalizes low PF. To improve PF to 0.95, what capacitance should be added in parallel? Assume 50 Hz, 400 V supply.

example.problem: Calculate required capacitor for PF improvement.
example.solution: Real power P = 100 kW (fixed). Initial: S_i = P / PF_i = 100 / 0.8 = 125 kVA. Q_i = √(S_i² − P²) = √(125² − 100²) = √(15625 − 10000) = √5625 = 75 kVAR. Target: S_t = 100 / 0.95 ≈ 105.3 kVA. Q_t = √(105.3² − 100²) ≈ 33 kVAR. Capacitor reactance needed: Q_C = Q_i − Q_t = 75 − 33 = 42 kVAR. X_C = V² / Q_C = (400)² / (42 × 10³) ≈ 3.8 Ω. C = 1 / (ωX_C) = 1 / (100π × 3.8) ≈ 840 μF. Result: Adding ~840 μF capacitor in parallel reduces monthly bill by ~20% (from 125 kVA to 105 kVA).

slides.title: Challenge: Resonance in a Radio Tuner

points.text: A radio tuner circuit has L = 50 μH and a variable capacitor C. To tune into FM station at 101.5 MHz, set resonance f₀ = 101.5 MHz. Assume R = 50 Ω (antenna resistance). Find C, Q, bandwidth Δf, and explain selectivity.

example.problem: Find C, Q, and bandwidth.
example.solution: Resonance: ω₀ = 2πf₀ = 2π × 101.5 × 10^6 rad/s. From ω₀ = 1/√(LC): C = 1 / (ω₀² L) = 1 / ((2π × 101.5 × 10^6)² × 50 × 10^-6) ≈ 4.9 × 10^-12 F ≈ 4.9 pF. At resonance: X_L = ω₀L = 2π × 101.5 × 10^6 × 50 × 10^-6 ≈ 31,800 Ω. Q = X_L / R = 31,800 / 50 ≈ 636. Bandwidth: Δf = f₀ / Q = 101.5 × 10^6 / 636 ≈ 159.6 kHz. Result: The tuner rejects stations outside 101.5 ± 80 kHz, isolating the target station from adjacent broadcasts.

slides.title: Resonance in Household AC Circuits
slides.storyContext: Anjali notices her microwave sometimes causes interference with her WiFi router when both run. 'That's because of resonance and harmonic injection,' her electrician father explains. 'The microwave's switching power supply draws non-sinusoidal current (harmonics). These harmonics leak into the WiFi band via electromagnetic coupling, causing interference. Proper filtering and shielding minimize this.'

slides.title: What You've Learned: Alternating Current

points.text: AC voltage V(t) = V₀ sin(ωt). RMS value V_rms = V₀/√2. Home voltage 230 V (RMS) ≈ 325 V (peak).
Impedance Z combines resistance R, inductive reactance X_L = 2πfL, and capacitive reactance X_C = 1/(2πfC).
Resonance at f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)): impedance Z = R (minimum), current I = V/R (maximum), phase φ = 0.
Real power P = V_rms I_rms cos(φ) is work done. Reactive power Q oscillates. Power factor PF = cos(φ).
Inductive loads lag (motors, lights). Capacitive loads lead (power factor correction capacitors).
Transformers step voltage up/down for efficient transmission. Power companies use 400 kV to minimize losses.
AC power reaches every home at 230 V, 50 Hz (India). Devices adapted for AC efficiency and safety.

slides.inSimpleWords: AC power oscillates 50 times per second. RLC circuits respond differently at different frequencies; resonance maximizes power transfer. Transformers enable long-distance transmission.

slides.title: Impedance in Complex Form

points.label: Impedance Z (complex number)
points.text: Z = R + jX = R + j(X_L − X_C), where j = √(−1). Magnitude |Z| = √(R² + X²). Phase angle φ = arctan(X/R).

points.label: Admittance Y
points.text: Y = 1/Z (complex conductance). Useful for parallel circuits where admittances add directly.

points.label: Power in complex form
points.text: S = V × I* (complex power, where I* is conjugate). Real part P = |S| cos(φ). Imaginary part Q = |S| sin(φ).

slides.inSimpleWords: Complex impedance combines R and X neatly. Math becomes simpler with phasors and complex numbers—used in all AC circuit analysis software.

slides.title: Worked Example: Parallel RC Circuit

example.problem: Parallel R = 100 Ω and C = 10 μF, driven at f = 50 Hz with V = 100 V. Find total current, power factor, and admittance.
example.solution: X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 50 × 10 × 10^-6) ≈ 318 Ω. Branch currents: I_R = V/R = 100/100 = 1 A (in phase). I_C = V × ωC = 100 × 2π × 50 × 10 × 10^-6 ≈ 0.314 A (leads by 90°). Total current (phasor): I = I_R + jI_C = 1 + j0.314. |I| = √(1² + 0.314²) ≈ 1.05 A. Phase: φ = arctan(0.314/1) ≈ −17.5° (leading, capacitive). Power factor: PF = cos(−17.5°) ≈ 0.95 (leading). Real power: P = 100 × 1 = 100 W.

slides.inSimpleWords: Parallel circuits: currents add as phasors. Capacitor branch leads; resistor is in phase. Total current phasor combined vectorially.

slides.title: Three-Phase AC and Power Distribution
slides.storyContext: Ravi takes Anjali to a power substation. 'See those three thick cables coming from the transmission line? That's three-phase AC—three sinusoids, 120° apart. Rotating at 50 Hz, they represent a rotating magnetic field. Induction motors sync to this rotating field and spin smoothly. Single-phase AC (home outlets) would make them vibrate. Three-phase is the backbone of industrial power.'

slides.title: Three-Phase AC Advantage

points.label: Three phases
points.text: V_a(t) = V₀ sin(ωt), V_b(t) = V₀ sin(ωt − 120°), V_c(t) = V₀ sin(ωt − 240°). Offset by 120° for continuous power delivery.

points.label: Rotating magnetic field
points.text: Three coils separated by 120° in space, carrying three-phase currents, create a rotating magnetic field. Motors sync to this rotation.

points.label: Efficiency
points.text: Constant power delivery (single-phase sags momentarily each cycle). Smaller, smoother, more efficient motors and generators.

slides.inSimpleWords: Three-phase AC provides continuous power via three offset sinusoids. Motors can sync to the rotating field and run smoothly without vibration.

slides.title: Worked Example: Induction Motor Efficiency

example.problem: A 5 kW, 3-phase induction motor (440 V, 50 Hz, PF = 0.85) draws current I = 8.5 A. Calculate apparent power, real power, reactive power, and efficiency considering copper loss (500 W) and core loss (300 W).
example.solution: Apparent power: S = √3 × V × I = 1.73 × 440 × 8.5 ≈ 6.46 kVA. Real power from circuit: P_in = S × PF = 6.46 × 0.85 ≈ 5.49 kW. Reactive power: Q = √(S² − P²) ≈ 3.79 kVAR. Total losses: P_loss = 500 + 300 = 800 W. Output power: P_out = P_in − P_loss = 5.49 − 0.8 = 4.69 kW (close to rated 5 kW, accounting for mechanical friction). Efficiency: η = P_out / P_in = 4.69 / 5.49 ≈ 85.4% (typical for industrial motors).

slides.inSimpleWords: Induction motors convert electrical power (real + reactive) into mechanical power minus losses (copper resistance + core losses). Efficiency typically 85–95%.

slides.title: Harmonic Distortion in AC Systems
slides.storyContext: Anjali's electrician father mentions 'harmonic pollution' in industrial power systems. 'Nonlinear loads like switched-mode power supplies and VFDs inject harmonic currents into the grid,' he explains. 'These are multiples of the fundamental 50 Hz (100 Hz, 150 Hz, etc.). They cause extra heating in cables, interfere with transformers, and waste energy.' Ravi: 'The fundamental frequency is sine; harmonics add distortion—like musical overtones.'

slides.title: Harmonics and Total Harmonic Distortion (THD)

points.label: Fourier series
points.text: Any periodic signal can be decomposed into sinusoids: V(t) = V_1 sin(ωt + φ_1) + V_3 sin(3ωt + φ_3) + V_5 sin(5ωt + φ_5) + ... (odd harmonics dominant)

points.label: Total Harmonic Distortion (THD)
points.text: THD = (√(V_3² + V_5² + V_7² + ...) / V_1) × 100%. For clean sine wave, THD ≈ 0%. Distorted waveforms, THD > 5% (problematic for sensitive equipment).

points.label: Sources of harmonics
points.text: Nonlinear loads: AC-DC converters, VFDs (variable frequency drives), LED drivers, fluorescent ballasts. Switching action creates harmonic currents.

slides.inSimpleWords: AC systems are supposed to be pure 50 Hz sinusoids, but nonlinear devices inject harmonics (3×, 5×, 7× the base frequency). This distortion wastes energy and damages equipment.

slides.title: AC Powers Modern Life
slides.storyContext: Anjali realizes that everywhere—in homes, factories, hospitals, trains—AC is doing the work. Not because it's simpler to understand (it's not!), but because it's simpler to generate (rotating coils), transmit (transformers), and distribute (step-down to homes). Every appliance with a plug adapts AC to what it needs: the charger converts to DC, the motor uses it directly, the heater dissipates it as heat. All because of Faraday's rotating coil and Nikola Tesla's three-phase AC insight. She texts her science club: 'We live in an AC world. But now I understand it!'

subject: Physics
title: Arjun's Radio Adventure: The Invisible Messenger
hook: Arjun builds a radio receiver and discovers the hidden waves that carry music across the city.

slides.title: Electromagnetic Waves: The Invisible Messenger
slides.storyContext: Arjun sits on his Mumbai apartment balcony, tuning an old radio. Static crackles, then suddenly a cricket commentary booms through the speaker. 'Where is this sound coming from?' he wonders. 'It's not a wire... it's flying through the air!' His teacher Kavya smiles. 'That's an electromagnetic wave, Arjun. Let's trace its journey.'

image.alt: Electromagnetic Waves: The Invisible Messenger — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: The World of Invisible Waves
slides.storyContext: Arjun lives in a city where radio broadcasts, mobile signals, WiFi, and TV signals fill the air invisibly. Every day, billions of waves carry information—cricket scores, Bollywood songs, news in Hindi and English—from towers to his radio, unseen. Kavya has challenged him: 'Build a simple radio tuner and explain how it catches one specific station from the electromagnetic chaos around you.' Arjun decides to understand the physics behind this magic.

image.alt: The World of Invisible Waves — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: What is an Electromagnetic Wave?
slides.storyContext: Kavya pulls out a diagram at her kitchen table. 'Imagine two dancers—Electricity and Magnetism. They dance perpendicular to each other, both perpendicular to the direction they're moving. That's an EM wave, Arjun. Neither electricity nor magnetism alone, but both oscillating together, pushing the wave forward at light speed.'

points.label: Definition
points.text: An electromagnetic wave is a self-propagating oscillation of perpendicular electric and magnetic fields. Both E and B oscillate perpendicular to the direction of propagation, and perpendicular to each other.

points.label: Speed in vacuum
points.text: All EM waves travel at c = 3 × 10^8 m/s ≈ 300,000 km/s in vacuum, regardless of frequency or wavelength. This speed is determined entirely by the constants of electric permittivity (ε₀) and magnetic permeability (μ₀).

points.label: No medium required
points.text: Unlike sound (which needs air or water), EM waves don't vibrate a physical medium—they ARE oscillating electric and magnetic fields. They propagate through empty space.

example.problem: A radio wave has a frequency of 100 MHz. What is its wavelength? Compare to visible light (500 nm).
example.solution: Radio wave: c = f λ, so λ = c/f = (3 × 10^8 m/s) / (100 × 10^6 Hz) = 3 m. Visible light: λ = 500 nm = 500 × 10^-9 m. Ratio: 3 m / (500 × 10^-9 m) = 6 × 10^9 (radio wavelength is 6 billion times longer than visible light!).

slides.inSimpleWords: An EM wave is electricity and magnetism dancing together through space at light speed. No medium needed—just oscillating fields creating each other.

image.alt: What is an Electromagnetic Wave? — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum
slides.storyContext: Vikram, the local radio broadcaster, invites Arjun to the studio. On the wall is a chart showing a rainbow of invisible waves. 'See,' Vikram points, 'your eyes see only a tiny slice—visible light. But our radio signal is far below. TV signals, microwaves, X-rays—all the same phenomenon, just different frequencies. The universe speaks to us in many wavelengths simultaneously.'

points.label: Spectrum order (low to high frequency)
points.text: Radio waves (kHz–GHz) → Microwaves (GHz) → Infrared (THz) → Visible light (400–700 nm) → Ultraviolet (UV) → X-rays → Gamma rays (high energy)

points.label: Wavelength-frequency relation
points.text: c = f × λ. Lower frequency = longer wavelength. Higher frequency = shorter wavelength, higher energy E = hf.

points.label: Radio waves: f ~ 10^3 to 10^10 Hz
points.text: λ ~ 10^5 to 10^-2 m. Used for AM/FM radio, TV, WiFi, cell phones, radar.

points.label: Visible light: f ~ 4–8 × 10^14 Hz
points.text: λ ~ 400–700 nm (nanometers). Only this tiny range can our eyes detect. Red (~700 nm), blue (~400 nm).

slides.inSimpleWords: Electromagnetic waves span from kilometers (radio) to picometers (gamma rays). Radio, visible light, X-rays—all identical waves, just different frequencies.

slides.title: Seeing Beyond Visible Light
slides.storyContext: Kavya shows Arjun thermal imaging: a person glowing with infrared heat. 'Your eyes can't see IR, but this camera can. A snake senses IR to hunt prey. Bees see ultraviolet flowers invisible to us. X-ray machines see through skin. Gamma rays from space would sterilize Earth if not for our magnetic field and atmosphere. All the same phenomenon, Arjun—just different frequencies. The universe is speaking to us in many wavelengths simultaneously. We're just blind to most of them.'

slides.title: Maxwell's Equations & Wave Equation
slides.storyContext: Kavya shows Arjun a picture of James Clerk Maxwell. 'In 1865, Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism mathematically. His four equations predicted that changing electric fields create magnetic fields, and vice versa. This mutual induction creates a self-sustaining wave traveling at light speed. Theoretical perfection! No one had made a radio yet, but physicists believed the math so strongly they knew EM waves must exist.'

points.label: Maxwell's key insight
points.text: ∂E/∂t creates B field. ∂B/∂t creates E field. They chase each other, creating a self-sustaining wave.

points.label: Wave equation solution
points.text: For E-field: ∂²E/∂t² = c² ∇²E. Solution: E(x,t) = E₀ sin(kx − ωt), where k = 2π/λ, ω = 2πf.

points.label: E and B relationship
points.text: E and B oscillate in phase (same sign at same time/place) and are perpendicular to each other. B₀ = E₀ / c always.

example.problem: EM wave: E₀ = 100 V/m, f = 50 MHz. Write E(x,t), find λ, k, ω, and B₀.

slides.inSimpleWords: Maxwell showed that electricity and magnetism create each other in a feedback loop. This loop propagates as a wave at light speed—no wires or medium needed.

image.alt: Maxwell's Equations & Wave Equation — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: Worked Example: Speed of Light from Maxwell's Constants

example.problem: From Maxwell's equations, EM wave speed c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀). Given ε₀ = 8.854 × 10^-12 F/m and μ₀ = 4π × 10^-7 H/m, calculate c and show it equals light speed.
example.solution: c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀) = 1/√((8.854 × 10^-12) × (4π × 10^-7)) = 1/√(1.111 × 10^-17) ≈ 3 × 10^8 m/s = 300,000 km/s. This matches the observed speed of light, proving light IS an EM wave. Maxwell's triumph!

slides.inSimpleWords: The constants of electricity and magnetism (ε₀ and μ₀) uniquely determine the speed of EM waves. This speed is light—confirming light is a wave phenomenon.

slides.title: Energy, Intensity, and Poynting Vector
slides.storyContext: Arjun asks Kavya: 'How much energy does a radio wave carry?' She smiles. 'Energy density—energy per cubic meter—comes from both electric and magnetic fields. And the direction of energy flow is given by the Poynting vector.'

points.label: Energy density
points.text: Total energy per unit volume: u = (1/2)(ε₀ E² + B²/μ₀). Electric and magnetic energy are equal.

points.label: Poynting vector
points.text: S = (1/μ₀) E × B (cross product). Direction of energy flow. Magnitude S = EB/μ₀ (W/m²).

points.label: Intensity
points.text: Time-averaged energy flux: I = <S> = (1/2μ₀c) E₀² = (ε₀c/2) E₀² (W/m²). Average power per unit area.

example.problem: EM wave with E₀ = 500 V/m. Calculate intensity and power intercepted by a 1 m² antenna.
example.solution: I = (ε₀c/2) E₀² = (8.85 × 10^-12 × 3 × 10^8 / 2) × (500)² ≈ 332.5 W/m². Power on 1 m² antenna: P = I × A = 332.5 × 1 ≈ 333 W (huge power!). But radio waves are typically much weaker ~10^-12 W/m² at receiver.

slides.inSimpleWords: EM waves carry energy in the direction they travel (Poynting vector). Intensity is average power per unit area. Strong broadcast stations have high intensity; weak distant signals have low intensity.

slides.title: Worked Example: Radio Antenna Design
slides.storyContext: Vikram wants to broadcast a new FM station at 101.5 MHz and asks Arjun for antenna advice. 'For maximum efficiency, the antenna should be about half the wavelength. What length?'

example.problem: Design antenna for 101.5 MHz. (a) Find wavelength. (b) Antenna length for resonance? (c) If transmitter outputs 5 kW, what intensity at 1 km distance?
example.solution: (a) λ = c/f = (3 × 10^8) / (101.5 × 10^6) ≈ 2.96 m. (b) Resonant length L ≈ λ/2 ≈ 1.48 m (half-wave dipole antenna—most efficient). (c) Power spreads isotropically over sphere radius 1 km: Area = 4πr² = 4π × (10^3)² ≈ 1.26 × 10^7 m². Intensity = 5000 / (1.26 × 10^7) ≈ 3.97 × 10^-4 W/m² ≈ 0.4 mW/m². This matches typical FM receiver sensitivity (~0.1 mW/m²).

image.alt: Worked Example: Radio Antenna Design — Electromagnetic Waves

slides.title: Polarization of EM Waves
slides.storyContext: Arjun adjusts the radio antenna—vertical, horizontal, diagonal. 'Why does signal change with angle?' Kavya smiles. 'The electric field oscillates in a fixed direction—vertical, horizontal, or any angle. That's polarization. Your antenna responds only to E-field oscillations along its axis. Mismatch the antenna orientation to the wave's polarization, and you get weak reception.'

points.label: Linear polarization
points.text: E-field vibrates in one fixed direction (e.g., vertical). Perpendicular antenna orientation reduces reception.

points.label: Brewster's angle and reflection
points.text: Polarization also affects wave reflection. Polarized light can be selectively reflected (e.g., by water) depending on angle.

points.label: Practical importance
points.text: Antenna orientation crucial for reception. Broadcast antennas polarize vertically or horizontally (or circularly). Receiver antennas must align.

slides.inSimpleWords: Polarization is the direction the E-field wiggles. Receiver antennas respond best when aligned with the wave's polarization. Mismatch = weak signal.

slides.title: Worked Example: Wavelengths of Different EM Waves

example.problem: Find wavelength and period for: (a) FM radio 100 MHz, (b) microwave 2.45 GHz, (c) UV light 3 × 10^15 Hz, (d) gamma ray 3 × 10^20 Hz.
example.solution: (a) λ = 3m, T = 10 ns. (b) λ ≈ 12.2 cm, T ≈ 0.41 ns. (c) λ = 100 nm, T ≈ 0.33 ps. (d) λ ≈ 1 pm, T ≈ 3.3 fs. The spectrum spans from kilometers to picometers, all traveling at light speed but with vastly different oscillation rates.

slides.inSimpleWords: All EM waves travel at light speed, but wavelength and frequency vary enormously. Radio: meters, slow oscillation. Gamma: picometers, ultrafast oscillation.

slides.title: Dispersion and Group Velocity

points.label: Phase velocity v_p
points.text: Speed at which wave crests move: v_p = ω / k = f λ. In dispersive media, v_p depends on frequency (color moves at different speeds).

points.label: Group velocity v_g
points.text: Speed at which wave energy (packet/envelope) travels: v_g = dω/dk. For information transfer, group velocity is relevant.

points.label: Anomalous dispersion
points.text: In some materials near resonance, v_g > v_p, or even v_g > c (but energy still travels at ≤ c).

slides.inSimpleWords: In normal materials, different colors travel at different speeds. Wave crests move at phase velocity; energy moves at group velocity (usually slower).

slides.title: Worked Example: Dispersion in Glass

example.problem: White light enters glass (n = 1.5 for red, 1.6 for blue). A prism disperses the light. Calculate the deflection angle difference between red and blue (prism angle 60°, incident angle 45°).
example.solution: Using Snell's law at first surface: sin(45°) = n sin(θ_r). Red: sin(θ_r) = 0.707/1.5 ≈ 0.471, θ_r ≈ 28.1°. Blue: sin(θ_b) = 0.707/1.6 ≈ 0.442, θ_b ≈ 26.2°. The blue ray bends more. At the second surface, further refraction and separation occur. Total angular separation ≈ 3–5° depending on geometry. This separation creates rainbow colors in prisms and water droplets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different colors refract differently in materials (dispersion). Blue bends more than red, separating white light into a spectrum—the basis of rainbows.

slides.title: Reflection and Transmission at Boundaries
slides.storyContext: Arjun observes water waves hitting a beach—some reflect, some transmit (refract into the sand). Kavya explains: 'EM waves do the same at dielectric boundaries. A portion reflects, a portion transmits (refracts). The ratio depends on refractive indices and angle of incidence. This is why radio waves reflect off buildings (metallic surfaces), why fiber optic cables confine light (total internal reflection), and why anti-reflection coatings work (destructive interference of reflected waves).'

slides.title: Reflection, Transmission, and Fresnel Equations

points.label: Fresnel reflection coefficient
points.text: r = (n₁ − n₂) / (n₁ + n₂) (normal incidence). Fraction of intensity reflected R = r². Transmitted intensity T = 1 − R.

points.label: Total internal reflection
points.text: When light travels from denser to less dense medium (e.g., glass to air) at angle > critical angle θ_c = arcsin(n₂/n₁), all light reflects. Exploited by fiber optics.

points.label: Anti-reflection coatings
points.text: Thin coating with n ≈ √(n_air × n_substrate) causes destructive interference of reflected waves, reducing reflection to <1%.

slides.inSimpleWords: EM waves partially reflect and partially transmit at interfaces between different materials. The ratio depends on refractive indices. Total internal reflection traps light in fiber optics.

slides.title: Electromagnetic Wave Propagation in Media
slides.storyContext: Kavya fills a tank with water and shines a light through it. 'Light slows down in water—c becomes c/n, where n is refractive index (~1.33 for water). Wavelength contracts, but frequency stays the same.' She explains: 'This is why objects underwater appear magnified. The bending of light (refraction) is actually EM waves slowing and bending at the air-water interface.'

slides.title: EM Waves in Different Media

points.label: Refractive index n
points.text: Speed of EM in medium: v = c/n. Wavelength in medium: λ_medium = λ_vacuum / n. Frequency unchanged (determined by source).

points.label: Snell's law
points.text: n₁ sin(θ₁) = n₂ sin(θ₂). EM wave bends when crossing interfaces between different n values.

points.label: Dispersion
points.text: For most materials, n depends on frequency. Higher frequency (blue) bends more than lower (red). This causes rainbows and prisms to separate white light.

slides.inSimpleWords: EM waves slow down in matter. The slower speed causes refraction (bending) at interfaces. Different frequencies bend differently—dispersion.

slides.title: Challenge: Microwave Oven Physics
slides.storyContext: Arjun's mother heats rice in a microwave. 'Why doesn't it heat the ceramic plate, only the food?' Kavya explains: 'Microwaves at 2.45 GHz match water molecule rotation frequency. Resonance! The food contains water, so it absorbs energy and heats. Ceramic doesn't absorb microwaves.' Arjun's challenge: compare microwave photon energy to visible light.

example.problem: Microwave oven at 2.45 GHz. (a) Find wavelength. (b) Photon energy (E = hf, h = 6.63 × 10^-34 J·s). (c) Compare to visible light (f ≈ 5 × 10^14 Hz). Why microwaves heat but visible light doesn't?
example.solution: (a) λ = c/f ≈ 12.2 cm. (b) E_mw = hf ≈ 1.62 × 10^-24 J ≈ 10^-5 eV (extremely low!). (c) E_visible ≈ 2 eV (10^5× higher). Yet microwaves heat while visible doesn't—why? Resonance! Water molecules rotate at GHz frequencies; microwave photons matching this frequency efficiently transfer energy. Visible photons are too energetic to couple to molecular rotation. Many weak photons (microwave) beat few strong photons (visible) for heating.

slides.title: Challenge: Radio Frequency Bandwidth and Communication

points.text: AM radio band: 530 kHz–1700 kHz. FM radio band: 88 MHz–108 MHz. (a) How many 10 kHz stations fit in AM band? (b) How many 200 kHz stations fit in FM band? (c) Why does FM have better sound quality but shorter range than AM?

example.problem: Calculate station capacity and explain quality-range tradeoff.
example.solution: (a) AM bandwidth = 1170 kHz; 1170/10 = 117 stations max. (b) FM bandwidth = 20 MHz; 20000/200 = 100 stations. (c) FM at 88–108 MHz (high freq) → short wavelength → absorbed/blocked by obstacles → limited range. AM at 530–1700 kHz (low freq) → long wavelength → diffracts around buildings → global range (via ionosphere bouncing). But AM's lower bandwidth (~5 kHz/station) limits audio quality (mono, poor treble). FM's wider bandwidth (~200 kHz/station) enables stereo and high-fidelity sound. Tradeoff: AM sacrifices quality for range; FM sacrifices range for quality.

slides.title: Recap: Electromagnetic Waves
slides.storyContext: Arjun now tunes his radio confidently. Kavya asks him to summarize. He takes a breath and explains:

points.text: EM waves are perpendicular oscillations of E and B fields, traveling at c = 3 × 10^8 m/s through space or any medium.
All EM waves related by c = f × λ. Lower frequency = longer wavelength (radio). Higher frequency = shorter wavelength (gamma).
The EM spectrum spans from radio (km) to gamma rays (pm). Visible light is a tiny 400–700 nm window.
Maxwell's equations predict EM waves and light. c = 1/√(ε₀μ₀) from first principles.
Energy transport: Poynting vector S = E × B / μ₀. Intensity I = (ε₀c/2) E₀². Measured in W/m².
Polarization: E-field oscillates in fixed direction. Antenna must align with polarization for best reception.
Applications: Radio, TV, WiFi, microwave ovens, medical imaging, radar, telecommunications. EM waves are the foundation of wireless technology.

slides.title: Doppler Shift in EM Waves
slides.storyContext: Arjun observes an ambulance with sirens wailing—the pitch drops as it passes. Kavya notes: 'Same phenomenon happens with EM waves: Doppler shift. A moving source compresses wavelengths (blueshifted) if approaching, stretches them (redshifted) if receding. Astronomers use this to detect if stars move toward or away from Earth. Police radar uses it to measure car speeds. Your favorite physics principle, applied to light!'

slides.title: Doppler Effect for EM Waves

points.label: Observer effect
points.text: If source moves toward observer at velocity v: observed f' = f × (c + v)/c (higher frequency, blueshift). If receding: f' = f × (c − v)/c (lower frequency, redshift).

points.label: Astrophysical applications
points.text: Hubble's redshift: distant galaxies' light redshifted → universe expanding. Quasar spectra redshifted → moving away at relativistic speeds.

points.label: Radar and police guns
points.text: Transmit radio wave at car. Reflected wave Doppler-shifted by 2× (target motion compresses wavelength, then it's reflected compressed further). f' = f × (1 + 2v/c).

slides.inSimpleWords: EM sources moving toward you shift to higher frequency (blueshift). Sources receding shift to lower frequency (redshift). This reveals motion and expansion of the universe.

slides.title: Worked Example: Optical Fiber Communication

example.problem: An optical fiber has core refractive index n_core = 1.48 and cladding n_cladding = 1.46. Light enters the fiber at 45° to the normal. Does total internal reflection occur at the core-cladding boundary? Calculate the critical angle.
example.solution: Critical angle: θ_c = arcsin(n_cladding / n_core) = arcsin(1.46/1.48) ≈ arcsin(0.9865) ≈ 80.4°. Light propagates down the fiber by bouncing off the core-cladding boundary. As long as incident angle (from fiber axis) exceeds θ_c, total internal reflection traps light. This is how fiber optics work: light 'bounces' inside the fiber, confined by total internal reflection, transmitting data over long distances with minimal loss.

slides.inSimpleWords: Optical fiber confines light via total internal reflection. Light bounces internally along the fiber, traveling kilometers with minimal loss—the backbone of internet communication.

slides.title: Applications Across the EM Spectrum

points.label: Radio waves (MHz)
points.text: AM/FM broadcasting, TV, WiFi, Bluetooth, cell phones. Long range, low frequency, easy to generate and transmit.

points.label: Microwaves (GHz)
points.text: Microwave ovens (heating), radar, satellite communication, 5G. Wavelength matches food molecules (water), enabling efficient heating.

points.label: Infrared (THz)
points.text: Thermal imaging, night vision, remote controls, fiber optics. Invisible to eye but detectable as heat.

points.label: Visible light (visible spectrum)
points.text: Eyes detect 400–700 nm. Photography, microscopy, communication via fiber optics, displays.

points.label: UV and beyond
points.text: Ultraviolet: sterilization, skin damage. X-rays: medical imaging. Gamma rays: nuclear processes, space astronomy.

slides.inSimpleWords: EM waves span 20+ orders of magnitude in frequency. Each part of spectrum has unique properties and applications. All governed by the same physics.

slides.title: EM Waves and Modern Communication
slides.storyContext: Arjun walks around Mumbai observing: WiFi routers broadcasting 2.4 GHz microwaves, cell towers broadcasting 4G/5G (1–4 GHz), GPS satellites transmitting at 1.2 and 1.6 GHz. All EM waves of different frequencies, coexisting in the same space, separated by tuned receivers that resonate at their frequency. A 21st-century miracle built on 19th-century physics. Maxwell's legacy surrounds us.

slides.title: The Invisible Network
slides.storyContext: Arjun stands on his balcony at sunset, radio in hand, and realizes: the words from his speaker traveled 40 km from Vikram's broadcast tower as a shimmering pattern of E and B fields, through buildings and trees, at 300,000 km/s. No wires, no physical connection—just Maxwell's equations made real. He texts Vikram: 'Got your 101.5 MHz wave!' and hears the time-delayed response: 'And your text arrived as radio waves too!' Waves crossing in the dark. That's wireless communication. That's the 21st century, running on physics discovered in the 19th. Arjun smiles: 'Maxwell figured this out 160 years ago. Genius.'
